chapters.title: The Gathering
paragraphs: As for what you're asking about, I believe I'm well prepared to answer. In fact, the day before yesterday I was on my way into the city from my home in Phalerum when an acquaintance of mine caught sight of me from behind and called out playfully from a distance, 'Apollodorus! You there — you Phalerian! Halt!' So I did as I was told, and he said, 'Apollodorus, I was just looking for you. I wanted to ask you about the speeches in praise of love that Socrates, Alcibiades, and others gave at Agathon's supper. Someone told me what he had heard from Phoenix, the son of Philip, but his account was very vague. He did say, though, that you knew about them, so I'd like to hear them from you. Who better than you to report your friend's words? But first tell me,' he said, 'were you at that gathering yourself?'
'Glaucon,' I said, 'your informant must have been very vague indeed, if you imagine that the occasion was recent, or that I could have been one of the party.'
'Well, yes,' he replied, 'I did think so.'

'Impossible,' I said. 'Don't you know that Agathon hasn't lived in Athens for many years, and that it's not yet three years since I started spending time with Socrates and made it my daily business to know everything he says and does? There was a time when I ran around from one thing to another, thinking I was doing something worthwhile, but I was really a thoroughly wretched creature — no better than you are now. I thought I ought to do anything rather than be a philosopher.'
'Well,' he said, 'joking aside, tell me when that gathering took place.'
'When we were still boys,' I replied, 'at the time Agathon won the prize with his first tragedy. It was the day after he and his chorus had offered their victory sacrifice.'
'Then it must have been a long time ago,' he said. 'And who told you — was it Socrates?'

'No, not Socrates,' I replied. 'It was the same man who told Phoenix — Aristodemus, of the deme of Cydathenaeum, a little fellow who never wore shoes. He had been at Agathon's feast, and I think that in those days no one was a more devoted admirer of Socrates. What's more, I have asked Socrates himself whether some parts of Aristodemus's account were true, and he confirmed them.' 'Then,' said Glaucon, 'let's hear the story. Isn't the road to Athens just made for conversation?' So we walked along and talked about the speeches on love. And that is why, as I told you at the start, I'm well prepared to do what you ask; I'll go through them again for you, if you like. For speaking about philosophy, or hearing others speak about it, always gives me the greatest pleasure — to say nothing of the benefit. But when I hear any other kind of talk — especially the talk of rich men and businessmen like you — it annoys me; and I pity you, my friends, because you think you're doing something when in reality you're doing nothing. I suppose you pity me in return and think I'm miserable — and very probably you're right. But what you only think about me, I know for certain about you. That's the difference.

COMPANION: I see you're just the same as ever, Apollodorus — always speaking ill of yourself and of others. I really do believe you pity all mankind except Socrates, starting with yourself. In this you live up to your old nickname, 'Apollodorus the madman.' I don't know how you came by it, but it suits you, for you're always raging against yourself and everybody except Socrates.
APOLLODORUS: Yes, friend, and the reason people say I'm crazy and out of my mind is precisely because I hold these views about you and about myself. No other evidence is needed.
COMPANION: Enough of that, Apollodorus. Let me renew my request and ask you to repeat the conversation for me.
APOLLODORUS: Well, the talk about love went like this — but perhaps I should start from the beginning and try to give you the exact words of Aristodemus.
He said that he had met Socrates fresh from the bath and wearing sandals. Since it was unusual to see Socrates in sandals, Aristodemus asked him where he was going all dressed up like a dandy.

'To a banquet at Agathon's,' he replied. 'I turned down his invitation yesterday — his victory sacrifice — because I was afraid of a crowd, but I promised to come today instead. So I've put on my finery, because he's such a fine man. What do you say — will you come along unasked?'
I replied, Aristodemus said, 'I'll do whatever you tell me.'
'Follow me, then,' he said, 'and let's demolish the proverb:'
'To the feasts of inferior men the good go uninvited;'
'and instead — since our host's name, Agathon, means "good" — our proverb will run:'
'To the feasts of the good the good go uninvited;'

'and we can support this change with the authority of Homer himself, who not only demolishes the proverb but does outright violence to it. For after portraying Agamemnon as the bravest of men, he has Menelaus, who is only a fainthearted warrior, come uninvited to Agamemnon's banquet while Agamemnon is feasting and offering sacrifices. So in Homer it is not the better who comes uninvited to the worse, but the worse to the better.'
'I'm rather afraid, Socrates,' said Aristodemus, 'that this may still be my case — that, like Menelaus in Homer, I shall be the inferior person who',
'To the feasts of the wise goes uninvited.'
'But I'll say that it was you who invited me, and then you'll have to come up with the excuse.'
'Two going together,'
he replied, in Homeric style, 'one or the other of them may think up an excuse on the way.'

This was the style of their conversation as they went along. Then Socrates, lost in thought, dropped behind and told Aristodemus, who had stopped to wait for him, to go on ahead. When Aristodemus reached Agathon's house, he found the doors wide open, and a comical thing happened. A servant coming out met him and led him straight into the dining hall, where the guests were reclining on their couches, for the banquet was about to begin. 'Welcome, Aristodemus,' said Agathon as soon as he appeared. 'You're just in time to have supper with us. If you've come about anything else, put it off and join us. I was looking for you yesterday — I meant to invite you, if only I'd been able to find you. But what have you done with Socrates?'
I turned around, Aristodemus said, but Socrates was nowhere to be seen. So I had to explain that he had been with me only a moment before, and that I had come to the supper at his invitation.
'You were quite right in coming,' said Agathon, 'but where is he himself?'
'He was behind me just now, as I entered,' he said, 'and I can't think what has become of him.'
'Go and look for him, boy,' said Agathon, 'and bring him in. And you, Aristodemus, take the place by Eryximachus in the meantime.'

The servant then helped him wash, and he took his place, reclining at the table. Soon another servant came in and reported that our friend Socrates had withdrawn into the porch of the house next door. 'He's standing there, rooted to the spot,' the servant said, 'and when I call him, he won't move.'
'How strange,' said Agathon. 'Then you must call him again, and keep calling him.'
'Let him alone,' said my informant, Aristodemus. 'He has a way of stopping anywhere and losing himself for no reason. I believe he will soon appear, so do not disturb him.'

'Well, if you think so, I'll leave him alone,' said Agathon. Then, turning to the servants, he added, 'Let's have supper without waiting for him. Serve whatever you like, since there's no one to give you orders — I've never left you to yourselves before. But this time, imagine that you are our hosts, and that I and the company are your guests. Treat us well, and we'll praise you for it.' After this, supper was served, but still there was no Socrates. During the meal Agathon said several times that he wanted to send for him, but Aristodemus objected. At last, when the feast was about half over — for his trance, as usual, did not last long — Socrates came in. Agathon, who was reclining alone at the end of the table, begged him to take the place next to him, 'so that I can touch you,' he said, 'and get the benefit of that wise thought that came to you in the porch and is now yours. For I'm certain you wouldn't have come away until you had found what you were looking for.'

'How I wish,' said Socrates, taking his place as he had been asked, 'that wisdom could flow by touch from the fuller man into the emptier, the way water creeps along a thread of wool from a fuller cup into an emptier one. If that were so, how highly I would value the privilege of reclining at your side! For you would fill me to the brim with a rich and beautiful stream of wisdom, whereas my own is a very poor and questionable sort, no better than a dream. But yours is bright and full of promise. The day before yesterday, in the theater, it shone out in all the splendor of youth before more than thirty thousand Greeks.'

'You're mocking me, Socrates,' said Agathon. 'Before long, you and I will have to settle which of us carries off the prize for wisdom, and Dionysus, god of wine and the theater, will be our judge. But for now, you'd better get on with your supper.'

Socrates took his place on the couch and ate supper with the others. Then they poured out offerings of wine to the gods, sang a hymn to the god, and went through the other customary rites. They were about to start drinking when Pausanias said, 'Now, my friends, how can we drink with the least harm to ourselves? I can tell you that I'm still suffering badly from yesterday's drinking and need time to recover — and I suspect most of you are in the same state, since you were at the party yesterday too. So think it over: how can we make the drinking as easy as possible?'
'I entirely agree,' said Aristophanes, 'that we should by all means avoid hard drinking, for I myself was one of the people who got drowned in drink yesterday.'
'I think you are right,' said Eryximachus, the son of Acumenus. 'But I'd still like to hear from one other person: is Agathon strong enough for hard drinking?'
'I'm not up to it,' said Agathon.

'In that case,' said Eryximachus, 'those of us who cannot hold our wine — myself, Aristodemus, Phaedrus, and others who can never drink much — are fortunate to find that the strong drinkers are not in the mood for drinking. I do not count Socrates: he can drink or abstain equally well, and will not mind whichever we do. Well, since none of the company seems inclined to drink much, I may be forgiven for saying, as a physician, that heavy drinking is a bad practice. I never indulge in it if I can help it, and I certainly do not recommend it to anyone else — least of all to someone who is still feeling the effects of yesterday's excesses.'
'I always do what you advise, and especially what you prescribe as a physician,' replied Phaedrus of Myrrhinus, 'and the rest of the company, if they are wise, will do the same.'
It was agreed that drinking was not to be the order of the day, but that they were all to drink only so much as they pleased.

'Then,' said Eryximachus, 'since you are all agreed that drinking is to be voluntary, and that no one is to be forced to drink, my next proposal is that the flute-girl, who has just come in, be told to go away and play to herself, or, if she likes, to the women inside the house. Today let us have conversation instead; and, if you will allow me, I will tell you what sort of conversation.' When this proposal had been accepted, Eryximachus went on as follows:
'I will begin,' he said, 'by borrowing Melanippe's line from a play by Euripides:'
'The word is not mine —'

'that I am about to speak, but Phaedrus's. For he often complains to me indignantly, "How strange it is, Eryximachus, that other gods have poems and hymns composed in their honor, while the great and glorious god Love has not a single poet to praise him, out of all the many poets there are. The worthy sophists too — professional teachers such as the excellent Prodicus — have written prose speeches praising the virtues of Heracles and other heroes. And what is even more extraordinary, I once came across a philosophical book in which the usefulness of salt was made the subject of an eloquent speech, and many other things like that have been honored in the same way. Just think: people have taken such an eager interest in things like these, and yet to this day no one has ever dared to sing Love's praises as he deserves! That is how completely this great god has been neglected." Now I think Phaedrus is quite right about this, and so I want to offer him a contribution. Besides, I think that at this moment we who are gathered here could do nothing better than honor the god Love. If you agree with me, there will be no shortage of conversation, because I propose that each of us in turn, going from left to right, should make a speech in honor of Love. Let each of us give the best speech he can; and Phaedrus should begin, because he is sitting first on the left, and because he is the father of the idea.'

'No one will vote against you, Eryximachus,' said Socrates. 'How could I oppose your motion, when the only subject I claim to understand is love? Nor, I imagine, will Agathon and Pausanias; and there's certainly no doubt about Aristophanes, the comic poet, whose whole concern is with Dionysus and Aphrodite — that is, with wine and the theater, and with love. Nor will anyone else I see around me disagree. I'm aware that the proposal may seem rather hard on those of us whose turn comes last, but we'll be content if we hear some good speeches first. Let Phaedrus begin the praise of Love, and good luck to him.' All the company agreed, and urged Phaedrus to do as Socrates had said.
Aristodemus did not remember everything that was said, and I do not remember everything he told me; but I will tell you what I thought most worth remembering, and what the chief speakers said.

chapters.title: Phaedrus's Speech
paragraphs: Phaedrus began by declaring that Love is a mighty god, wonderful among gods and men, but especially wonderful in his birth. For he is the eldest of the gods, which is an honor to him; and a proof of his claim to this honor is that there is no record of his parents. No poet or prose writer has ever said that he had any. As the poet Hesiod says:
'First Chaos came, and then broad-bosomed Earth, the everlasting seat of all that is, and Love.'
In other words, after Chaos, these two came into being: Earth and Love. And the philosopher-poet Parmenides sings of Generation, the power that brings things into being, as the maker of Love:
'He fashioned Love, the first of all the gods.'

And Acusilaus, an early prose writer on the origins of the gods, agrees with Hesiod. So there are many witnesses who acknowledge that Love is the eldest of the gods. And he is not only the eldest; he is also the source of the greatest benefits to us. For, Phaedrus said, I know of no greater blessing for a young man who is starting out in life than a virtuous lover — an older man who loves and courts him — and no greater blessing for the lover than a beloved youth. For there is a principle that ought to guide men who want to live nobly, and I say that neither family, nor public honors, nor wealth, nor any other motive can instill that principle as well as love can. What do I mean? The sense of honor and dishonor, without which neither states nor individuals ever do any good or great work. And I say that if a lover is caught doing something dishonorable, or letting someone else dishonor him because he is too cowardly to defend himself, he will be more pained to be seen by his beloved than by his father, his companions, or anyone else. The beloved, too, when he is caught in any disgraceful situation, feels the same way about his lover. So if only there were some way to form a state or an army made up of lovers and their beloveds, they would be the very best governors of their own city, holding back from everything dishonorable and competing with one another for honor. And fighting side by side, even a mere handful of them would overcome the world.

For what lover would not rather be seen by the whole of mankind than by his beloved when he was deserting his post or throwing away his weapons? He would be ready to die a thousand deaths rather than endure that. Or who would desert his beloved, or fail him in the hour of danger? At such a time even the worst coward would become an inspired hero, equal to the bravest — Love would inspire him. Homer says that a god breathes courage into the souls of some heroes; Love, by his very nature, gives that same courage to the lover.

Love, and love alone, will make men dare to die for their beloved — and women as well as men. Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, stands as proof of this before all Greece. Her husband could escape death only if someone would die in his place, and she was willing to lay down her life for him when no one else would, although he had a father and a mother. But her love was so much tenderer than theirs that she made them seem like strangers to their own son, as if they were not his own flesh and blood but related to him in name only. And her deed seemed so noble, to the gods as well as to men, that of the many who have done noble deeds, she is one of the very few to whom the gods, in admiration of what she did, have granted the privilege of coming back alive to earth from the dead. That is how highly the gods honor devotion and virtue in love. But when Orpheus the harper, the son of Oeagrus, went down to Hades for his dead wife, the gods sent him away empty-handed. They showed him only a phantom of the woman he had come for, and would not give her up herself, because he showed no spirit. He was only a harp-player, and did not dare, as Alcestis did, to die for love; instead, he schemed to find a way into Hades while still alive. What is more, the gods later had him put to death at the hands of women, as the punishment for his cowardice.

Very different was the reward Achilles received for his true love toward Patroclus, who was his lover and not his beloved — that is, Patroclus was the older man who loved him, and Achilles the younger man he loved. The idea that Patroclus was the beloved is a foolish mistake made by the tragic poet Aeschylus, for Achilles was surely the more beautiful of the two, and more beautiful than all the other heroes too; and, as Homer tells us, he was still beardless and much younger. The gods do greatly honor the virtue of love; but they admire, value, and reward it even more when the beloved returns the love of his lover, for the lover is more divine than the beloved, since he is inspired by a god. Now Achilles knew very well, because his mother had told him, that if he held back from killing Hector — the Trojan who had killed Patroclus — he could escape death, return home, and live to a ripe old age. Nevertheless he gave his life to avenge his friend: he dared not only to die for him, but to die after him, when Patroclus was already dead. That is why the gods honored him even above Alcestis, and sent him to the Islands of the Blessed, the paradise of heroes. These are my reasons for declaring that Love is the eldest, the noblest, and the mightiest of the gods, and the chief author and giver of virtue in life and of happiness after death.

chapters.title: Pausanias's Speech
paragraphs: This, or something close to it, was Phaedrus's speech. Several other speeches followed that Aristodemus couldn't remember, but the next one he recounted was Pausanias's. Pausanias began: Phaedrus, I don't think the question has been framed correctly. We shouldn't be asked to praise Love in such an undiscriminating way. If there were only one Love, what you said would be fine — but since there are more Loves than one, we should have started by deciding which of them we are praising. Let me fix this oversight. First I'll tell you which Love deserves our praise, and then I'll try to praise him in a manner worthy of him. For we all know that Love is inseparable from Aphrodite, and if there were only one Aphrodite there would be only one Love — but since there are two goddesses, there must be two Loves. And am I not right that there are two goddesses? The elder, who has no mother, is called the heavenly Aphrodite — she is the daughter of Uranus, god of the heavens. The younger, the daughter of Zeus and Dione, we call Common, the Aphrodite of all the people; and the Love who works alongside her is rightly named Common, just as the other Love is called Heavenly. All the gods deserve praise, but not without distinguishing their natures — so I must try to distinguish the characters of the two Loves. Now, actions vary in value according to how they are performed.

Take, for example, what we are doing right now — drinking, singing, and talking. These actions are not in themselves either good or evil; they turn out one way or the other depending on how they are done. Done well, they are good; done badly, they are evil. In the same way, not every love is noble and worthy of praise — only the love that has a noble purpose. The Love who is the offspring of the Common Aphrodite is essentially common and makes no distinctions. It is the love the baser sort of men feel, directed equally at women and at youths, and it is of the body rather than the soul. Its objects are the most foolish people, since this love cares only about getting what it wants and never about achieving its end nobly, and so it does good and evil quite indiscriminately. The goddess who is his mother is far younger than the other, and she was born of the union of male and female, and so has something of both. But the offspring of the Heavenly Aphrodite comes from a mother in whose birth the female had no part — she is from the male only. This is the love that is directed toward youths, and because the goddess is older, there is nothing lewd or unruly in her. Those inspired by this love turn to the male, delighting in whoever has the more valiant and intelligent nature; and anyone can recognize those who are purely inspired by this love from the very character of their attachments.

For they love not boys, but young people whose minds are beginning to develop — around the age when their beards begin to grow. And in choosing young men as their companions, they mean to be faithful to them, to spend their whole lives with them — not to catch them in their inexperience, deceive them, make fools of them, or run from one to another. The love of young boys, however, ought to be forbidden by law, because their future is uncertain: they may turn out good or bad, in body or soul, and much noble enthusiasm may be wasted on them. In this matter the good are a law to themselves, but the coarser sort of lovers ought to be restrained by force — just as we try to restrain them from fixing their affections on freeborn women. These are the people who give love a bad name; and some have been led to deny that such attachments can ever be proper, because they see the impropriety and evil in them. But surely nothing done in an orderly and lawful way can justly be blamed.

Now here in Athens, and in Lacedaemon, the rules about love are perplexing, but in most cities they are simple and easy to grasp. In Elis and Boeotia, and in countries that have no gift for eloquence, the rules are very straightforward — the law is simply in favor of these connections, and no one, young or old, says a word against them. The reason, I suppose, is that the men there are not eloquent, so lovers prefer not to take the trouble of pleading their case. In Ionia, on the other hand, and in other places generally subject to the barbarians, the custom is held to be dishonorable. There, love between males shares the evil reputation attached to philosophy and gymnastics, because all three are hostile to tyranny. Rulers' interests require that their subjects be poor in spirit and that no strong bond of friendship or fellowship form among them — and love, more than any other motive, is likely to inspire such bonds, as our own Athenian tyrants learned by experience. For Aristogeiton's love and Harmodius's constancy proved strong enough to bring down their power.

And so the ill repute into which these attachments have fallen in some places must be attributed to the bad character of those who condemn them — that is, to the self-seeking of the rulers and the cowardice of the ruled. On the other hand, the indiscriminate honor given to them in other countries comes from the mental laziness of those who hold that opinion. In our own country a far better principle prevails, though, as I said, it's a rather perplexing one. Consider: open loves are held to be more honorable than secret ones, and the love of the noblest and highest is especially honorable, even when the beloved is less beautiful than others. Consider too the enormous encouragement the whole world gives the lover: he is not thought to be doing anything dishonorable — if he wins his beloved he is admired, and if he fails he is thought disgraced. And in pursuing his love, custom allows him to do many strange things that philosophy would bitterly condemn if they were done from any motive of profit, or desire for office, or power.

He may pray, beg, plead, swear oaths, sleep on a mat at the door, and endure a servitude worse than any slave's. In any other situation his friends and enemies alike would step in to stop him; but here no friend will be ashamed of him or admonish him, and no enemy will accuse him of servility or flattery. The actions of a lover have a grace that ennobles them, and custom has decided they are highly commendable and bring no loss of character. And strangest of all, he alone may swear an oath and break it — so people say — and the gods will forgive his transgression, for there is no such thing as a lover's oath. Such is the complete liberty that gods and men have allowed the lover, according to the custom that prevails in our part of the world. From this point of view a man could reasonably argue that in Athens to love and to be loved is considered a most honorable thing. But then consider the other side. Fathers forbid their sons to talk with their lovers and put them in the care of a tutor whose job is to prevent any such thing; their companions and friends of their own age taunt them if they see anything of the sort; and their elders do not silence these taunts or scold those who make them. Anyone reflecting on all this would conclude, on the contrary, that we hold these practices to be utterly disgraceful.

But as I was saying at the start, the truth, I think, is this: whether such practices are honorable or dishonorable is not a simple question. They are honorable to whoever pursues them honorably, and dishonorable to whoever pursues them dishonorably. There is dishonor in yielding — that is, in a beloved's granting physical favors — to a bad lover, or in yielding in a bad way; but there is honor in yielding to a good lover, or in yielding in an honorable way. And the bad lover is the common lover, inspired by the Common Love, who loves the body rather than the soul; for he is not even stable, since he loves something that is itself unstable. So when the bloom of youth he desired is over, he takes wing and flies away, despite all his words and promises. But the man who loves a noble character stays for life, because his love becomes one with what is everlasting. The custom of our country wants both kinds of lover to be tested well and truly, and wants the beloved to yield to the one sort and avoid the other. That is why it encourages lovers to pursue and the beloved to flee: it tests both lover and beloved in contests and trials, until each of them shows which of the two kinds he belongs to.

This is why, in the first place, a hasty attachment is considered dishonorable: time is the true test, here as in most other things. And secondly, there is dishonor in being overcome by the love of money, wealth, or political power — whether a man is frightened into surrender by the fear of losing them, or, having tasted the benefits of money and political corruption, cannot rise above their seductions. For none of these things is permanent or lasting, and besides, no generous friendship ever sprang from them. There remains, then, only one honorable way, allowed by custom, for the beloved to yield — the way of virtue. For just as we granted that any service the lover renders to his beloved is not to be counted as flattery or as a dishonor to himself, so the beloved has one, and only one, form of voluntary service that is not dishonorable: namely, virtuous service.

For we have a custom according to which, if someone serves another in the belief that he will be improved by him — whether in wisdom or in some other particular of virtue — such voluntary service is not to be considered a dishonor, and it is not open to the charge of flattery. These two customs — the love of youth, and the practice of philosophy and virtue generally — ought to meet in one; and when they do, the beloved may honorably yield to the lover. For when lover and beloved come together, each following his own law: the lover thinking he is right to do any service he can for his gracious loved one, and the beloved thinking he is right to show any kindness he can to the one who is making him wise and good — the first capable of communicating wisdom and virtue, the second seeking to acquire them for the sake of his education and wisdom — then, when the two laws of love are fulfilled and meet in one, and only then, may the beloved yield honorably to the lover. And when love is of this disinterested sort, there is no disgrace in being deceived; but in every other case there is equal disgrace in being deceived or not. For if someone yields to a lover under the impression that he is rich, and is then disappointed of his gains because the lover turns out to be poor, he is disgraced just the same — because he has done his best to show that he would give himself up to anyone's 'uses base' for the sake of money; and that is not honorable.

By the same principle, a man who gives himself to a lover because he believes him to be a good man, hoping to be improved by his company, shows himself to be virtuous even if the object of his affection turns out to be a scoundrel with no virtue at all. If he is deceived, his error is a noble one. For he has proved that on his side he will do anything for anyone with a view to virtue and self-improvement — and nothing can be nobler than that. So it is noble in every case to yield to a lover for the sake of virtue. This is the love of the Heavenly Goddess — heavenly love, of great worth to individuals and to cities, making lover and beloved alike earnest in the work of their own improvement. All other loves are the offspring of the other goddess, the Common one. To you, Phaedrus, I offer this contribution of mine in praise of Love, the best I could make on short notice.

Pausanias came to a pause — there's a neat little jingle for you, in the balanced style the wise teachers of speaking have taught me. Aristodemus said that Aristophanes was due to speak next, but either because he had eaten too much or for some other reason, he had the hiccups and had to switch turns with Eryximachus the physician, who was reclining on the couch below him. 'Eryximachus,' said Aristophanes, 'you ought either to stop my hiccups or to speak in my place until they're over.'

'I'll do both,' said Eryximachus. 'I'll speak in your place, and you can speak in mine; and while I'm speaking, let me recommend you hold your breath. If after a while the hiccups haven't gotten better, then gargle a little water; and if they still persist, tickle your nose with something and sneeze — once or twice should do it, and even the most violent hiccups are sure to stop.' 'I'll do as you prescribe,' said Aristophanes. 'Now get on with it.'

chapters.title: Eryximachus's Speech
paragraphs: Eryximachus spoke as follows: 'Since Pausanias made a fine beginning but a lame ending, I must try to supply what he left out. I think he was right to distinguish two kinds of love. But my own art, medicine, informs me further that this double love is not merely a feeling in human souls, directed toward beautiful people or toward anything else. It is also found in the bodies of all animals, in all that grows from the earth, and, I may say, in everything that exists. That is the conclusion I seem to have drawn from my own art of medicine, which teaches me how great and wonderful and universal a god Love is: his empire extends over all things, divine as well as human. And I will begin with medicine, to honor my own art. The human body contains these two kinds of love. Everyone agrees that they are different and unlike, and because they are unlike, what they love and desire is unlike too: what is healthy desires one thing, and what is diseased desires another. Pausanias said a moment ago that it is honorable to gratify good men — to yield to their love — and dishonorable to gratify bad ones. In the same way, in the body the good and healthy elements should be gratified, while the bad elements, the elements of disease, should not be gratified but discouraged.

'This is what the physician has to do, and this is what the art of medicine consists of. For medicine can be regarded, broadly speaking, as the knowledge of the body's loves and desires, and of how to satisfy them or not. The best physician is the one who can separate the beautiful love from the ugly, or turn one into the other. And a physician who knows how to root out love and how to plant it, whichever is needed, and who can reconcile the most hostile elements in the body's constitution and make them loving friends, is a skillful practitioner. Now the most hostile elements are the most opposite ones, such as hot and cold, bitter and sweet, moist and dry, and the like. My ancestor Asclepius — we doctors trace our descent from him — knew how to plant friendship and agreement in these elements, and so he created our art. That is what our poet friends here tell us, and I believe them. And not only medicine in all its branches, but also the arts of physical training and farming, are under Love's dominion. Anyone who gives the subject the slightest attention will also see that music involves the same reconciling of opposites. I suppose that must have been what the philosopher Heraclitus meant, although he did not put it accurately. For he says that the One is united by disunion, like the harmony of the bow and the lyre, in which string and frame pull against each other and so hold together. Now it is absurd to say that harmony is discord, or that it is made up of elements that are still in a state of discord.

'But what he probably meant was this: harmony is made of differing notes, of higher and lower pitch, that once disagreed but have now been reconciled by the art of music. For if the higher and lower notes still disagreed, there could be no harmony — clearly not. After all, harmony is consonance, that is, notes sounding together; and consonance is an agreement. But there can be no agreement between things that disagree, as long as they still disagree: you cannot harmonize what disagrees. In the same way, rhythm is made up of short and long beats, which once differed but are now in accord. And just as medicine plants this agreement in the body, so music plants it in all these cases, making love and unison grow up among them. So music, too, is concerned with the principles of love, as they apply to harmony and rhythm. Again, if you look at harmony and rhythm in their essential nature, it is easy to make out love in them, and there love has not yet become double: it has not yet split into a good kind and a bad kind. But when you want to use them in actual life, either in composing songs or in correctly performing melodies and verses already composed — which is what we call education, since that is how the young are trained — then the difficulty begins, and a good artist is needed.

'At that point the same argument comes back: the argument about the beautiful and heavenly love, which in music is the love that comes from Urania, the beautiful and heavenly Muse, one of the goddesses of the arts. It says that it is our duty to gratify people who are self-controlled, and to gratify those who are not yet self-controlled only so that they may become self-controlled, and to preserve their love. And again it tells of Polyhymnia, the common Muse of many songs, who stands in music for the Common Love. She must be used with caution, so that her pleasure is enjoyed without breeding debauchery — just as in my own art it is no small task to regulate a gourmet's appetites, so that he can satisfy his tastes without the disease that comes with them. From this I conclude that in music, in medicine, and in all other things, human as well as divine, we must keep watch on both loves as far as we can, for both are present.

'The course of the seasons, too, is full of both these principles. When, as I was saying, the elements of hot and cold, moist and dry, come to feel a harmonious love for one another and blend with moderation and harmony, they bring health and plenty to men, animals, and plants, and do them no harm. But when the unruly love gets the upper hand and takes hold of the seasons of the year, it does great damage and harm. It is the source of plagues, and it brings many other kinds of disease on animals and plants; for frost, hail, and blight all spring from the excesses and disorders of these elements of love. The study of these elements of love, as they relate to the movements of the heavenly bodies and to the seasons of the year, is called astronomy. Furthermore, all sacrifices, and the whole field of divination — the reading of signs from the gods, the art through which gods and men communicate — are concerned, I say, only with preserving the good love and curing the bad. For every kind of impiety is likely to follow if, instead of yielding to, honoring, and revering the harmonious love in everything he does, a man honors the other love, whether in his feelings toward gods or parents, toward the living or the dead. That is why the task of divination is to watch over these loves and heal them; and divination is the peacemaker between gods and men, working through its knowledge of the pious and impious tendencies in human loves. Such is the great and mighty — or rather, the all-powerful — force of love in general.

'And above all, it is the love concerned with the good that has the greatest power — the love that is perfected in company with self-control and justice, whether among gods or men. This love is the source of all our happiness and harmony, and it makes us friends with the gods above us and with one another. I suppose that I too have left out several things that might be said in praise of Love, but this was not intentional. And now, Aristophanes, you may make up for what I have omitted, or praise him in some other way; for I see that you are rid of your hiccups.'

'Yes,' said Aristophanes, who was next to speak, 'the hiccups are gone — though not until I applied the sneeze. And I wonder whether the harmony of the body has a love for such noises and ticklings, since no sooner had I applied the sneeze than I was cured.'

Eryximachus said: 'Take care, my friend Aristophanes. You are about to speak, and yet you are making fun of me. So I shall have to keep an eye on your speech and see whether I can have a laugh at your expense, when you could otherwise speak in peace.'

'You are right,' said Aristophanes, laughing. 'I take back what I said. But please don't watch me, because I'm afraid that in the speech I am about to make, instead of people laughing with me — which comes naturally to our comic muse and would be all to the good — they will only laugh at me.'

'Do you think you can take your shot and get away with it, Aristophanes?' said Eryximachus. 'Well, perhaps if you are very careful and bear in mind that you will be called to account, I may be persuaded to let you off.'

chapters.title: Aristophanes's Speech
paragraphs: Aristophanes announced that he would take the discussion in a new direction: he meant to praise Love in a different way from either Pausanias or Eryximachus. 'Mankind,' he said, 'has never understood the power of Love at all, in my view — you can tell from the way people neglect him. If they had understood him, they would surely have built him noble temples and altars and offered solemn sacrifices in his honor. None of this is done, though it most certainly ought to be — for of all the gods, Love is the best friend of human beings: he is our helper, and the healer of the ills that are the greatest obstacle to the happiness of our race. I will try to explain his power to you, and you must pass on to the rest of the world what I am teaching you. First, let me explain human nature and what has happened to it, because our original nature was not the same as it is now, but different. Originally there were not two sexes, as there are now, but three: man, woman, and a union of the two. This third sex had a name to match its double nature. It once really existed but has now been lost, and its name, "Androgynous," meaning man-woman, survives only as an insult. Second, the original human beings, of all three kinds, were round, their backs and sides forming a circle. Each of them had four hands and four feet, and one head on a round neck, with two faces, exactly alike, looking in opposite directions. Each also had four ears, two sets of genitals, and everything else to match.

'They could walk upright, as people do now, backwards or forwards as they pleased. But they could also roll over and over at great speed, turning on their four hands and four feet, eight limbs in all, like acrobats turning cartwheels, going over and over with their legs in the air; that was how they ran when they wanted to go fast. There were three sexes, of the kinds I have described, because the sun, the moon, and the earth are three. The man was originally the child of the sun, the woman the child of the earth, and the man-woman the child of the moon, which shares in both sun and earth; and they were all round, and moved round and round, like their parents. Their strength and might were terrifying, their pride and ambition were enormous, and they launched an attack on the gods. They are the ones in the story of Otys and Ephialtes, the two brothers who, as Homer says, dared to climb up to heaven and would have laid hands on the gods. The gods met in council in heaven and could not decide what to do. If they killed them and wiped out the whole race with thunderbolts, as they had once done to the giants, there would be an end of the sacrifices and worship that humans offered them. But on the other hand, the gods could not let such arrogance go unchecked. At last, after a great deal of thought, Zeus found a way. He said: "I think I have a plan that will humble their pride and improve their manners. Humans will go on existing, but I will cut each of them in two. Then they will be weaker in strength and greater in number, which will also have the advantage of making them more profitable to us.

'"They will walk upright on two legs. And if they are still arrogant and will not keep quiet, I will split them again, and they can hop about on one leg." With that, he cut the humans in two, the way a sorb-apple, a small fruit, is halved for pickling, or the way you might slice an egg with a hair. As he cut them, one after another, he told Apollo to twist each one's face and half its neck around toward the cut side, so that the person could look at where he had been cut and learn a lesson in humility. Apollo was also told to heal their wounds and reshape their bodies. So Apollo turned the face around, and pulled the skin in from the sides over what we call the belly, gathering it like a drawstring purse. He made a single opening in the middle and tied it off in a knot, the one we call the navel. He also shaped the chest and smoothed out most of the wrinkles, much as a shoemaker smooths leather over a last, the foot-shaped block he works on. But he left a few wrinkles around the belly and navel, as a reminder of our original state. Once they had been cut in two, each half longed for its other half, and the halves came together. They threw their arms around one another, entwined in each other's embrace, longing to grow back into one; and they were on the point of dying of hunger and self-neglect, because they did not want to do anything apart. And when one half died and the other survived, the survivor looked for another mate — a man or a woman, as we call them now, though each was really only half of a whole man or a whole woman — and clung to that one.

'They were dying out when Zeus took pity on them and came up with a new plan. He moved their genitals round to the front, where they had not always been. Until then they had sown their seed not in one another but in the ground, the way grasshoppers lay their eggs in the earth; from then on they sowed it in one another. After this change, the male reproduced in the female, so that when a man and a woman embraced they would have children, and the race would continue; or, if a man came together with a man, they would be satisfied, and could rest, and get on with the business of life. That is how ancient our inborn desire for one another is. It brings our original nature back together, making one out of two and healing the human condition. Each of us, once separated and left with only one side, like a flatfish, is only half of a human being, like one half of a token split in two that matches nothing but its partner; and each of us is always looking for his other half. Men who are halves of the double being once called Androgynous are lovers of women; most adulterers come from this stock, and so do adulterous women who lust after men. Women who are halves of an original woman do not care for men, but are drawn to women; women who take other women as lovers are of this kind. But those who are halves of an original male pursue males. While they are young, being slices of the original man, they hang around men and embrace them; and they are the best of boys and young men, because they have the most manly nature.

'Some people say that they are shameless, but that is not true. They do not behave this way from any lack of shame, but because they are brave and manly and have a manly look, and they embrace what is like themselves. And when they grow up, these are the men who become our statesmen, and they are the only ones who do, which is strong proof that what I am saying is true. As grown men they are lovers of youths — that is, they court younger men — and by nature they are not inclined to marry or have children. If they do so at all, it is only because law and custom require it; they are content to live with one another unmarried, if they are allowed to. A man of this nature is quick to love and ready to return love, always embracing what is akin to him. And when one of them meets his other half, the actual half of himself, whether he is a lover of youths or a lover of some other kind, the pair are lost in amazement, overcome by love and friendship and intimacy, and neither will let the other out of his sight even for a moment, so to speak. These are the people who spend their whole lives together, and yet they could not explain what they want from each other. For the intense longing each feels for the other does not seem to be a desire for sexual union, but for something else. The soul of each clearly desires something it cannot put into words, something it senses only darkly and doubtfully.

'Suppose Hephaestus, the blacksmith god, came with his tools to the pair as they lay side by side, and asked them, "What is it you people want from each other?" They would not be able to explain. And suppose further that, seeing how puzzled they were, he said: "Do you want to be wholly one, always together, day and night? Because if that is what you want, I am ready to melt you into one and let you grow together, so that the two of you will become one. As long as you live, you will share a single life, as if you were one person; and after you die, down in the world below, you will still be one departed soul instead of two. So I ask you: is this what your love desires, and would you be satisfied to have it?" Every one of them, on hearing this offer, would agree, and not one would deny, that this meeting and melting into one another, this becoming one instead of two, was the very expression of his age-old need. And the reason is that human nature was originally one and we were a whole, and the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love. There was a time, I say, when we were one; but now, because of the wickedness of humankind, the god has dispersed us, just as the Lacedaemonians, that is, the Spartans, dispersed the Arcadians into villages.

'And if we do not obey the gods, there is a danger that we will be split in two again and go about like the flat figures carved in profile on monuments, with only half a nose; and that we will be like tallies, those tokens split in two whose halves match only each other. So let us urge everyone to show reverence toward the gods, in order that we may avoid evil and obtain the good, which Love rules over and brings to us. And let no one oppose Love: whoever opposes him is an enemy of the gods. For if we are friends of the god and at peace with him, we will find the loves that are truly our own, which rarely happens in this world at present. I am being serious, so I must beg Eryximachus not to make fun of this, or to find in what I am saying any allusion to Pausanias and Agathon, who, I suspect, are both of the manly kind and belong to the class I have been describing. But my words apply more widely: they include men and women everywhere. And I believe that if our loves were perfectly fulfilled, and each of us, returning to his original nature, won his own original true love, then our race would be happy. And if that would be best of all, then the next best thing, as things are now, must be whatever comes nearest to that union: finding a love whose nature is truly akin to our own.

'So if we want to praise the one who has done us this good, we must praise the god Love, our greatest benefactor. In this life he leads us back to our own nature, and he gives us high hopes for the future, for he promises that if we are reverent toward the gods, he will restore us to our original state, and heal us, and make us happy and blessed. This, Eryximachus, is my speech about love. It is different from yours, but I must beg you not to make it a target for your jokes, so that each of the others may have his turn — each, or rather either, since Agathon and Socrates are the only ones left.'

'Indeed, I am not going to attack you,' said Eryximachus, 'for I thought your speech charming. If I did not know that Agathon and Socrates are masters in the art of love, I would be really afraid that they would have nothing left to say, after the vast number of things that have been said already. But even so, I have hopes.'
Socrates said: 'You played your part well, Eryximachus. But if you were in my position now, or rather in the position I will be in once Agathon has spoken, you would indeed be completely at a loss.'
'You want to cast a spell over me, Socrates,' said Agathon, 'hoping that I will lose my nerve because the audience has been led to expect that I will speak well.'

'Agathon,' replied Socrates, 'I would have to be strangely forgetful to think that a small party of friends could rattle your nerves. I remember the courage and greatness of spirit you showed when your own plays were about to be performed: you came up onto the stage with the actors and faced that vast theater without the least dismay.'
'Do you think, Socrates,' said Agathon, 'that my head is so full of the theater that I don't know how much more a man of sense fears a few good judges than a crowd of fools?'

'No,' replied Socrates, 'I would be very wrong, Agathon, to attribute that or any other lack of refinement to you. And I am well aware that if you met people you thought wise, you would care much more about their opinion than about the opinion of the many. But then we cannot be counted among the select few who are wise, since we were part of the foolish many in the theater. Still, I know that if you happened to find yourself in the presence, not of one of us, but of someone truly wise, you would be ashamed to disgrace yourself in front of him — wouldn't you?'
'Yes,' said Agathon.
'But in front of the many, you would not be ashamed if you thought you were doing something disgraceful?'

Here Phaedrus interrupted them, saying: 'Do not answer him, my dear Agathon; for if he can only get a partner to talk with, especially a good-looking one, he will no longer care about finishing our plan. Now, I love to hear him talk; but just at present I must not forget the speech in praise of Love — what we call an encomium — which he and everyone else owe me. When you and he have paid your tribute to the god, then you may talk.'
'Very good, Phaedrus,' said Agathon. 'I see no reason not to go on with my speech, since I shall have many other chances to talk with Socrates. Let me first say how I ought to speak, and then speak:'

chapters.title: Agathon's Speech
paragraphs: The speakers before me, instead of praising the god Love or revealing his nature, seem to have congratulated mankind on the benefits he bestows on them. But I would rather praise the god first, and then speak of his gifts; that is always the right way to praise anything. May I say, without irreverence or offense, that of all the blessed gods Love is the most blessed, because he is the most beautiful and the best? And he is the most beautiful, first of all because he is the youngest. He himself is the witness of his own youth, for he flees from Old Age — and Old Age is swift enough, swifter, truly, than most of us would like. Love hates Old Age and will not come near him; but youth and love live and move together, for, as the proverb says, like is drawn to like. Phaedrus said many things about Love that I agree with; but I cannot agree that Love is older than Iapetus and Kronos, the ancient Titans. Not so! I maintain that he is the youngest of the gods, and forever young. The ancient doings among the gods, those deeds of divine violence that the poet Hesiod and the philosopher-poet Parmenides told of, were, if the stories are true, the work of Necessity, the power of compulsion, and not of Love. Had Love been there in those days, there would have been no chaining or mutilating of gods, and no other violence, but peace and sweetness, as there is now in heaven, ever since Love began to reign. Love is young, and he is also tender. He deserves a poet like Homer to describe his tenderness, the way Homer says of Ate, the goddess of ruin, that she is a goddess and tender:
'Her feet are tender, for she sets her steps not on the ground but on the heads of men:'

Here is excellent proof of her tenderness: she walks not on what is hard, but on what is soft. Let me offer a similar proof of the tenderness of Love. He walks not on the earth, nor even on the skulls of men, which are not so very soft, but in the hearts and souls of both gods and men, which are the softest things of all: in them he walks and dwells and makes his home. Yet not in every soul without exception; for where there is hardness he departs, and where there is softness, there he dwells. And since he always nestles, with his feet and in every other way, in the softest of soft places, how can he be anything but the softest of all things? Truly, then, he is the tenderest as well as the youngest; and he is also supple in form. For if he were hard and unbending, he could not wrap himself around all things, or wind his way unnoticed into and out of every human soul. And proof of his suppleness and the fine proportions of his form is his grace, which everyone agrees belongs to Love in a special way; gracelessness and love are forever at war with each other. The beauty of his coloring is shown by his home among the flowers. For he does not live among beauties that have no bloom or are fading, whether of body or soul or anything else; but wherever there are flowers and scents, there he settles, and there he stays. About the beauty of the god I have said enough — and yet there is much more that I could say.

Now I must speak of his virtue. His greatest glory is that he can neither do wrong to any god or any man, nor suffer wrong from any god or any man. The reason is that if anything is done to him, it is not done by force, since force never comes near him; and when he acts, he does not act by force. For everyone serves Love in everything of their own free will, and where there is willing agreement, there, as the laws that are the lords of the city declare, is justice. So he is just; and not only just, but supremely self-controlled. For self-control is acknowledged to be the ruler of the pleasures and desires, and no pleasure ever masters Love: he is their master, and they are his servants. And if he conquers them, he must be self-controlled indeed. As for courage, even Ares, the God of War, is no match for him. Ares is the captive and Love is the lord; for love, his love for Aphrodite, masters him, as the story goes; and the master is stronger than the servant. And if Love conquers the bravest of all the others, he himself must be the bravest. I have spoken of his courage and justice and self-control; but I have yet to speak of his wisdom, and I must try to do my best, as far as my ability allows. In the first place, he is a poet — and here, like Eryximachus, I am praising my own art — and he is also the source of poetry in others, which he could not be if he were not a poet himself.

At his touch, everyone becomes a poet, even one who had no music in him before; and this too is proof that Love is a good poet, accomplished in all the fine arts, for no one can give another what he does not have himself, or teach what he does not know. Who will deny that the creation of the animals is his doing? Are they not all works of his wisdom, conceived and born through him? And as for the artists, do we not know that only the one whom Love inspires comes into the light of fame, while the one whom Love never touches walks in darkness? Apollo discovered the arts of medicine and archery and divination under the guidance of love and desire, so he too is a disciple of Love. So too the melody of the Muses, the metalwork of Hephaestus, the weaving of Athene, and the rule of Zeus over gods and men are all owed to Love, who invented them. And so Love set the realm of the gods in order — the love of beauty, clearly, for Love has nothing to do with ugliness. In the old days, as I said at the start, dreadful deeds were done among the gods, because they were ruled by Necessity; but ever since Love was born, every good thing in heaven and on earth has sprung from the Love of the beautiful. Therefore, Phaedrus, I say of Love that he is himself the most beautiful and the best, and the cause of all that is most beautiful and best in everything else. And a line of poetry comes into my mind in which he is said to be the god who
'Gives peace on earth and calms the stormy deep, who stills the winds and bids the sufferer sleep.'

This is he who empties men of disaffection and fills them with affection, who brings them together at banquets such as these; in sacrifices, feasts, dances, he is our lord — who sends courtesy and sends away discourtesy, who gives kindness ever and never gives unkindness; the friend of the good, the wonder of the wise, the amazement of the gods; desired by those who have no part in him, and precious to those who have the better part in him; parent of delicacy, luxury, desire, fondness, softness, grace; regardful of the good, regardless of the evil; in every word, work, wish, fear — savior, pilot, comrade, helper; glory of gods and men, leader best and brightest; in whose footsteps let every man follow, sweetly singing in his honor and joining in that sweet song with which love charms the souls of gods and men. Such is the speech, Phaedrus, half-playful yet having a certain measure of seriousness, which, according to my ability, I dedicate to the god.

When Agathon had finished speaking, Aristodemus said that everyone cheered; the young man was thought to have spoken in a way worthy of himself and of the god. And Socrates, looking at Eryximachus, said: 'Tell me, son of Acumenus, was I not right to be afraid? And was I not a true prophet when I said that Agathon would make a wonderful speech, and that I would be at a loss?'
'The part of the prophecy about Agathon,' replied Eryximachus, 'seems to me to be true; but not the other part — that you will be at a loss.'

'Why, my dear friend,' said Socrates, 'wouldn't I, or anyone, be at a loss, having to speak after hearing such a rich and varied speech? I am especially struck by the beauty of the closing words — who could listen to them without amazement? When I thought how immeasurably inferior my own powers are, I was ready to run away in shame, if there had been any way to escape. For the speech reminded me of Gorgias, the famous orator; and at its end I imagined Agathon shaking at me the Gorginian — or should I say Gorgonian — head of that great master of rhetoric. Like the head of the monster Gorgon, it was meant simply to turn me and my speech to stone, as Homer says, and strike me dumb. And then I realized how foolish I had been to agree to take my turn with you in praising love, and to say that I too was a master of the art, when in fact I had no idea how anything ought to be praised. For in my simplicity I imagined that whatever is said in praise should be true; and that, with truth as the starting point, the speaker should choose the finest of these truths and set them out in the best way. And I felt quite proud, thinking that I knew the nature of true praise and would speak well. But now I see that the idea was to credit Love with every kind of greatness and glory, whether it really belonged to him or not, without regard to truth or falsehood — that did not matter. For the original proposal, it seems, was not that each of you should really praise Love, but only that you should appear to praise him.

'And so you attribute to Love every imaginable form of praise that can be gathered from anywhere; and you say that "he is all this," and "the cause of all that," making him appear the most beautiful and best of all to people who do not know him — for you cannot fool those who do. And what a noble, solemn hymn of praise you have delivered! But since I misunderstood the nature of the praise when I said that I would take my turn, I must beg to be released from the promise I made in ignorance, which, as Euripides would say, was a promise of the lips and not of the mind. So goodbye to that style of praise, for I do not praise in that way — no, indeed, I cannot. But if you would like to hear the truth about love, I am ready to speak in my own manner, though I will not make myself ridiculous by entering into any rivalry with you. So tell me, Phaedrus, whether you would like to hear the truth about love, spoken in whatever words and in whatever order happen to come into my mind at the time. Would that suit you?'

Aristodemus said that Phaedrus and the others told Socrates to speak in whatever way he thought best. 'Then,' Socrates added, 'let me first have your permission to ask Agathon a few more questions, so that I can build my argument on the points he agrees to.'
'You have my permission,' said Phaedrus. 'Ask your questions.' Socrates then went on as follows:

chapters.title: Socrates & Diotima
paragraphs: 'In the magnificent speech you have just given, my dear Agathon, I think you were right to propose speaking first of the nature of Love and afterwards of his works — that is a way of beginning I very much approve of. And since you have spoken so eloquently of his nature, may I ask you something further: is love the love of something, or of nothing — does it always have an object? Here I must explain myself. I am not asking whose child Love is, as though he were the love of some father or mother; that would be a ridiculous question. I am asking the kind of thing I would be asking if I said: is a father the father of something? You would have no difficulty in replying that he is the father of a son or a daughter, and that answer would be right.'
'Very true,' said Agathon.
'And you would say the same of a mother?'
He assented.
'Let me ask you one more question to make my meaning clear: isn't a brother, by his very nature, the brother of something?'
'Certainly,' he replied.
'That is, of a brother or sister?'
'Yes,' he said.
'And now,' said Socrates, 'I will ask about Love: Is Love of something, or of nothing?'
'Of something, surely,' he replied.
'Keep in mind what it is that love loves — hold that answer back for now — and tell me just this: does Love desire the thing he loves?'
'Yes, surely.'
'And does he have the thing he loves and desires, or not?'
'Probably not, I'd say.'

'No,' replied Socrates, 'I'd like you to consider whether "necessarily," and not "probably," is the right word. The inference that he who desires something lacks something, and that he who desires nothing lacks nothing, is in my judgment, Agathon, absolutely and necessarily true. What do you think?'
'I agree with you,' said Agathon.
'Very good. Would someone who is great desire to be great, or someone who is strong desire to be strong?'
'That would contradict what we have already agreed.'
'True. For if someone already is something, he cannot lack it?'
'Very true.'

'And yet,' added Socrates, 'suppose a man who is strong desires to be strong, or a man who is swift desires to be swift, or a man who is healthy desires to be healthy. In that case he might be thought to desire something he already has, or already is. I give this example so that we do not fall into a misunderstanding. For we must suppose, Agathon, that people who possess these qualities have their advantages at the present moment, whether they like it or not; and who can desire what he already has? So when someone says, "I am well and wish to be well," or "I am rich and wish to be rich, and I desire simply to have what I have," we shall reply to him: "My friend, you have wealth and health and strength, and what you want is to go on having them; for at this moment, whether you like it or not, you have them. So when you say that you desire what you have and nothing else, don't you really mean that you want to have in the future what you have now?" He must agree with us — mustn't he?'
'He must,' replied Agathon.

'Then,' said Socrates, 'what he desires is that what he has now should be kept for him in the future — which is the same as saying that he desires something that does not yet exist for him, something he does not yet have.'
'Very true,' he said.

'Then he, and everyone else who desires, desires what he does not already have, what lies in the future and not in the present, what he does not possess, what he is not, and what he lacks. So these are the kinds of things that love and desire seek?'
'Very true,' he said.
'Now then,' said Socrates, 'let us sum up the argument. First, is love not the love of something — and of something, too, that one lacks?'
'Yes,' he replied.

'Remember, too, what you said in your speech — or if you do not remember, I will remind you. You said that the love of the beautiful set the realm of the gods in order, because there is no love of ugly things. Didn't you say something like that?'
'Yes,' said Agathon.
'Yes, my friend, and you were right to say so. And if this is true, Love is the love of beauty and not of ugliness?'
He assented.
'And we have already agreed that love is the love of what one lacks and does not have?'
'True,' he said.
'Then Love lacks beauty, and does not have it?'
'Certainly,' he replied.
'And would you call that beautiful which lacks and does not possess beauty?'
'Certainly not.'
'Then would you still say that Love is beautiful?'
Agathon replied: 'I fear that I did not understand what I was saying.'
'You made a very good speech, Agathon,' replied Socrates, 'but there is still one small question I would like to ask: isn't what is good also beautiful — fine and noble?'
'Yes.'
'Then in lacking the beautiful, Love also lacks the good?'
'I cannot refute you, Socrates,' said Agathon. 'Let us assume that what you say is true.'
'No, beloved Agathon — it is the truth that you cannot refute, for Socrates is easily refuted.

'And now I will leave you in peace, and tell a story about love that I heard from Diotima of Mantineia, a woman wise in this and in many other kinds of knowledge. Long ago, when the Athenians offered sacrifices before the plague came, she delayed the disease for ten years. She was my teacher in the art of love, and I shall repeat to you what she said to me. I will begin with the points Agathon admitted, which are nearly, if not quite, the same as those I admitted to the wise woman when she questioned me. I think this will be the easiest way, and I shall take both parts myself, hers and mine, as well as I can. As you suggested, Agathon, I must speak first of the being and nature of Love, and then of his works. First I said to her in nearly the same words that Agathon used to me: that Love was a mighty god, and beautiful as well. And she proved to me, just as I proved to him, that by my own argument Love was neither beautiful nor good. "What do you mean, Diotima?" I said. "Is love then bad and ugly?" "Hush," she cried. "Must whatever is not beautiful be ugly?" "Certainly," I said. "And is whatever is not wise ignorant?" she asked. "Do you not see that there is something in between wisdom and ignorance?" "And what might that be?" I said.

'"Right opinion," she replied. "As you know, right opinion means being right without being able to give a reason for it. So it is not knowledge, for how can there be knowledge without reason? Nor is it ignorance, for ignorance can never arrive at the truth. Clearly, then, it is something in between ignorance and wisdom." "Quite true," I replied. "Then do not insist," she said, "that whatever is not beautiful must be ugly, or that whatever is not good must be bad. And do not conclude that because love is not beautiful and good, he must therefore be ugly and bad; for he is in between them." "Well," I said, "surely Love is admitted by everyone to be a great god." "By those who know, or by those who do not know?" she asked. "By everyone." "And how, Socrates," she said with a smile, "can Love be admitted to be a great god by those who say that he is not a god at all?" "And who are they?" I said. "You and I are two of them," she replied. "How can that be?" I said. "It is easy to see," she replied, "for you yourself would admit that the gods are happy and beautiful — of course you would. Would you dare to say that any god was not?" "Certainly not," I replied. "And by the happy, you mean those who possess good or beautiful things?" "Yes." "And you admitted that Love, because he lacks good and beautiful things, desires the very things he lacks?" "Yes, I did." "But how can he be a god if he has no share in what is good or beautiful?" "Impossible." "Then you see that you too deny that Love is a god."

'"What then is Love?" I asked. "Is he mortal?" "No." "What then?" "As in the earlier case, he is neither mortal nor immortal, but in between the two." "What is he, Diotima?" "He is a great spirit, and like all spirits he is midway between the divine and the mortal." "And what," I said, "is his power?" "He interprets," she replied, "between gods and men. He carries the prayers and sacrifices of men across to the gods, and brings the commands and replies of the gods to men. He is the mediator who spans the gulf that divides them, and so in him everything is bound together. Through him the arts of the prophet and the priest find their way, with their sacrifices and mysteries and charms, and all prophecy and incantation. For a god does not mix with a human being; all communication and conversation between gods and men, whether men are awake or asleep, is carried on through Love. The wisdom which understands this is spiritual; all other wisdom, such as that of the arts and crafts, is lowly and workaday. Now these spirits, or in-between powers, are many and of many kinds, and one of them is Love." "And who," I said, "was his father, and who was his mother?" "The story," she said, "will take time; but I will tell you all the same. On Aphrodite's birthday the gods held a feast, and one of the guests was the god Poros, whose name means Plenty or Resource; he is the son of Metis, Cunning Intelligence. When the feast was over, Penia, or Poverty, came to the door to beg, as beggars do at a feast.

'"Now Plenty, who was drunk on nectar (there was no wine in those days), went into the garden of Zeus and fell into a heavy sleep. And Poverty, thinking of her own hard circumstances, plotted to have a child by him; so she lay down at his side and conceived Love. Love is Aphrodite's follower and attendant, partly because he is by nature a lover of the beautiful, and because Aphrodite is herself beautiful, and also because he was born on her birthday. His fortunes match his parentage. In the first place, he is always poor, and far from being tender and beautiful, as most people imagine him. He is rough and dirty, with no shoes and no house to live in. He sleeps on the bare ground, exposed under the open sky, in the streets or in doorways; and like his mother he is always in need. But he also partly resembles his father, and like him he is always scheming to win the beautiful and the good. He is bold, enterprising and strong, a mighty hunter, always weaving some intrigue or other, keen in the pursuit of wisdom, full of resources; a philosopher at all times, and formidable as an enchanter, a sorcerer and a sophist, one of those clever professional teachers of wisdom. By nature he is neither mortal nor immortal: at one moment, when he has plenty, he is alive and flourishing; at another he is dead; and then he comes alive again, because of his father's nature.

'"But whatever flows in to him is always flowing out again, and so he is never destitute and never rich; and he is also in between ignorance and knowledge. The truth of the matter is this: no god is a philosopher, a seeker after wisdom, for he is wise already; nor does any man who is wise seek after wisdom. Neither do the ignorant seek after wisdom. For this is what is bad about ignorance: someone who is neither good nor wise is nevertheless satisfied with himself, and he has no desire for what he does not feel he lacks." "But who, then, Diotima," I said, "are the lovers of wisdom, if they are neither the wise nor the foolish?" "A child could answer that question," she replied. "They are those who are in between the two, and Love is one of them. For wisdom is one of the most beautiful things, and Love is love of the beautiful; and so Love is also a philosopher, a lover of wisdom, and as a lover of wisdom he is in between the wise and the ignorant. His birth explains this too, for his father is rich and wise, and his mother poor and foolish. Such, my dear Socrates, is the nature of the spirit Love. Your mistaken idea of him was very natural. From what you say, I imagine it came from confusing love with the beloved — what loves with what is loved — and that made you think that love was entirely beautiful. For it is the beloved who is truly beautiful, and delicate, and perfect, and blessed; but what loves has a different nature, the one I have described."

'I said, "Well said, my friend from Mantineia. But if Love is as you say, what use is he to men?" "That, Socrates," she replied, "I will try to explain. I have already spoken of his nature and his birth, and you agree that love is love of the beautiful. But someone may ask us both, 'Socrates and Diotima, what is it about the beautiful that love wants?' Or rather, let me put the question more clearly: when a man loves the beautiful, what does he desire?" I answered her, "That the beautiful may be his." "Still," she said, "that answer raises a further question: what does possessing beauty give him?" "I have no answer ready for that question," I replied. "Then," she said, "let me put the word 'good' in place of the beautiful, and ask the question once more: if a man loves the good, what does he desire?" "The possession of the good," I said. "And what does someone who possesses the good gain?" "Happiness," I replied. "That question is easier to answer." "Yes," she said, "the happy are made happy by acquiring good things. And there is no need to ask why a man desires happiness; that answer is already final." "You are right," I said.

'"And is this wish, this desire, common to all? Do all men always desire their own good, or only some men? What do you say?" "All men," I replied. "The desire is common to all." "Then why, Socrates," she asked, "do we not say that all men are in love, instead of saying that only some are? For you say that all men are always loving the same things." "I wonder about that myself," I said. "There is nothing to wonder at," she replied. "The reason is that one part of love is separated off and given the name of the whole, while the other parts have other names." "Give me an example," I said. She answered me as follows: "Take poetry, which, as you know, is complex and takes many forms. Our word for poetry literally means 'making': every act of creation, every passage from not-being into being, is poetry, or making. The processes of all the arts are creative, and so the masters of all the arts are poets, or makers." "Very true." "Still," she said, "you know that they are not called poets, but have other names. Only one part of the art, which is separated off from the rest and is concerned with music and meter, is called poetry; and only those who have poetry in this sense of the word are called poets." "Very true," I said. "And the same holds for love.

'"For you may say, in general, that every desire for good things and for happiness is simply the great and subtle power of love. But those who are drawn to him by some other path, whether the path of making money, or athletics, or philosophy, are not called lovers. Only those whose love takes one particular form, the love of one person for another, are given the name that belongs to the whole: they alone are said to love, or to be lovers." "You are probably right," I replied. "Yes," she added, "and you hear people say that lovers are seeking their other half. But I say that they are seeking neither the half of themselves nor the whole, unless that half or whole is also something good. And men will cut off their own hands and feet and throw them away, if they think those limbs are bad. For people do not love what is their own just because it is their own — unless perhaps someone calls whatever belongs to him good, and whatever belongs to another bad. For there is nothing that men love but the good. Is there anything else?" "Certainly not, I should say." "Then," she said, "the simple truth is that men love the good." "Yes," I said. "And to this we must add that they love the possession of the good?" "Yes, that must be added." "And not only the possession, but the everlasting possession of the good?" "That must be added too."
