"Then love," she said, "may be described in general as the love of the everlasting possession of the good?" "That is most true."

'"Then if this is the nature of love," she said, "can you tell me further how it is pursued? What are they doing, those who show all this eagerness and heat that is called love? And what is the goal they have in view? Answer me." "No, Diotima," I replied. "If I had known, I would not have marveled at your wisdom, or come to learn from you about this very thing." "Well," she said, "I will teach you. The goal they have in view is birth in beauty — giving birth in the presence of beauty — whether of body or of soul." "I do not understand you," I said. "It would take a prophet to know what you mean." "I will make my meaning clearer," she replied. "I mean that all human beings are pregnant — they carry something within them that is waiting to be born — in body and in soul. At a certain age human nature desires to procreate — and procreation must take place in beauty, not in ugliness. This procreation is the union of man and woman, and it is a divine thing; for conception and reproduction are something immortal in a mortal creature, and they can never happen in what is out of harmony with the divine. But the ugly is always out of harmony with the divine, and the beautiful is in harmony with it.

'"Beauty, then, is the goddess of destiny and of childbirth who presides over birth. So when a pregnant creature comes near beauty, it becomes gracious; it relaxes and opens; it is kindly, and it gives birth and bears fruit. But at the sight of ugliness it frowns and contracts and feels pain; it turns away and shrivels up, and, not without a pang, holds back from giving birth. That is why, when the time comes and the pregnant creature is full to bursting, there is such a flutter and ecstasy about beauty, because the approach of beauty relieves the pains of labor. For love, Socrates, is not, as you imagine, love of the beautiful only." "What then?" "The love of reproduction and of birth in beauty." "Yes," I said. "Yes, indeed," she replied. "But why is love the love of reproduction? Because for a mortal creature, reproduction is a kind of eternity and immortality. And if, as we have already agreed, love is the love of the everlasting possession of the good, then all men must necessarily desire immortality together with the good. So love is also the love of immortality."

'All this she taught me at various times when she spoke about love. And I remember her once saying to me, "What is the cause, Socrates, of love and of the desire that goes with it? Do you not see how all animals, birds as well as beasts, are in agony when they catch the infection of love in their desire to reproduce? It begins with the desire to mate; then comes care for their young, for whose sake the weakest are ready to fight the strongest to the utmost, and to die for them, and will let themselves be tormented by hunger or suffer anything else in order to provide for their young. Man, one may suppose, acts like this from reason; but why should animals have these passionate feelings? Can you tell me why?" Again I replied that I did not know. She said to me, "And do you expect ever to become a master in the art of love, if you do not know this?" "But I have told you already, Diotima, that my ignorance is the reason I come to you; for I know that I need a teacher. So tell me the cause of this, and of the other mysteries of love." "If you believe that love is the love of the immortal, as we have agreed several times," she said, "then do not be surprised. For here again, and on the same principle, mortal nature is seeking, as far as it can, to be everlasting and immortal; and it can achieve this only by reproduction, because reproduction always leaves behind a new existence in place of the old.

'"Indeed, even in the life of a single individual there is succession, not complete sameness. A man is called the same person; and yet in the short time between youth and old age, the time in which every living creature is said to be alive and to remain the same, he is going through a constant process of loss and renewal: his hair, flesh, bones, blood and whole body are always changing. And this is true not only of the body but also of the soul. Our habits, tempers, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains and fears never stay the same in any of us, but are always coming and going. It is equally true of knowledge; and, what is still more surprising to us mortals, not only do whole branches of knowledge spring up and decay in us, so that we are never the same with respect to them, but each single piece of knowledge undergoes the same change. For what does the word 'recollection' — calling knowledge back to mind — imply, if not that knowledge departs? Knowledge is always being forgotten, and it is renewed and preserved by recollection, so that it seems to be the same although in reality it is new. That is the law of succession by which all mortal things are preserved: not by remaining exactly the same, but by replacement, the old and worn-out mortal thing leaving behind another that is new and similar. The divine is different; it is always the same and never another. In this way, Socrates, the mortal body, or anything else mortal, shares in immortality; but what is immortal is immortal in another way.
'"So do not be surprised at the love that all men have for their children; for that universal love and concern is for the sake of immortality."

'I was astonished at her words, and said, "Is this really true, wise Diotima?" And she answered with all the authority of an accomplished sophist, one of those professional teachers of wisdom: "Of that, Socrates, you may be sure. Just think of the ambition of men, and you will be amazed at how senseless their ways are, unless you consider how they are stirred by the love of an immortal fame. They are ready to run all kinds of risks, far greater than they would have run for their children, and to spend money, and undergo any sort of toil, and even to die, for the sake of leaving behind them a name that will be eternal. Do you imagine that Alcestis would have died to save Admetus, or Achilles to avenge Patroclus, or your own Codrus, an early king of Athens, to preserve the kingdom for his sons, if they had not imagined that the memory of their virtues, which still lives on among us, would be immortal? Indeed," she said, "I am convinced that all men do everything they do in the hope of the glorious fame of immortal virtue, and the better they are, the more they do so; for they desire the immortal.

'"Those who are pregnant in body only turn to women and have children — this is the form their love takes. Their children, they hope, will preserve their memory and give them the blessedness and immortality that they desire in the future. But souls that are pregnant — for there certainly are men who are more creative in their souls than in their bodies — conceive what it is fitting for the soul to conceive and carry. And what are these conceptions? Wisdom and virtue in general. And such creators are the poets, and all the artists who deserve the name of inventor. But by far the greatest and most beautiful kind of wisdom is the one concerned with the ordering of states and families, which is called self-control and justice. And when a man has had the seed of these planted in him from his youth, and is himself inspired, then when he comes to maturity he desires to reproduce and to give birth.

'"He wanders about seeking beauty so that he may give birth to offspring — for in ugliness he will give birth to nothing — and so he naturally embraces beautiful bodies rather than ugly ones. Above all, when he finds a soul that is beautiful and noble and well brought up, he embraces the two, body and soul, in one person. To such a person he talks freely about virtue, and about what a good man is and how he should live; and he tries to educate him. And through contact with the beautiful one, who is always present in his memory even when absent, he gives birth to what he conceived long ago, and together with him he nurtures what he has brought forth. And so the two of them are married by a far closer bond, and share a closer friendship, than those who have mortal children together, for the children they have in common are more beautiful and more immortal. Who, when he thinks of Homer and Hesiod and the other great poets, would not rather have their children than ordinary human ones? Who would not want to rival them in creating children like theirs, which have preserved their memory and given them everlasting glory? Or who would not want such children as the lawgiver Lycurgus left behind him in his laws, to be the saviors not only of Lacedaemon, that is, Sparta, but of Hellas, the whole of Greece, as one might say?

'"There is Solon, too, the revered father of Athenian law; and there are many others in many other places, both among Hellenes and among barbarians — Greeks and non-Greeks alike — who have given the world many noble works and have been the parents of every kind of virtue. Many temples have been raised in their honor for the sake of children such as theirs; but no temple was ever raised in anyone's honor for the sake of his mortal children.

'"These are the lesser mysteries of love, the first rites of initiation, into which even you, Socrates, may enter. Then there are the greater and more hidden mysteries, the final rites, which are the crown of these; and the lesser mysteries, if you pursue them in the right spirit, will lead you to them. Whether you will be able to attain to those, I do not know. But I will do my utmost to teach you, and you must follow if you can. For whoever would go about this matter rightly should begin in youth by turning to beautiful bodies. First, if the one who guides him through these mysteries leads him rightly, he should love one such body only, and out of that love he should create beautiful thoughts. Soon he will see for himself that the beauty of one body is akin to the beauty of another. And then, if beauty of body in general is what he pursues, how foolish he would be not to recognize that the beauty in all bodies is one and the same! When he sees this, he will relax his intense passion for the one, looking down on it and thinking it a small thing, and he will become a lover of all beautiful bodies. In the next stage he will consider the beauty of the mind more precious than outward, bodily beauty.

'"So even if someone with a virtuous soul has only a little physical beauty, he will be content to love him and care for him, and will seek out and give birth to thoughts that may make the young better, until he is compelled to contemplate and see the beauty of institutions and laws, and to understand that the beauty of them all is of one family, and that bodily beauty is a small thing. After laws and institutions he will go on to the branches of knowledge, so that he may see their beauty. He will not be like a servant in love with the beauty of one young man, or one man, or one institution, himself a slave, petty and narrow-minded. Instead, turning toward the vast sea of beauty and contemplating it, he will create many beautiful and noble thoughts and notions in a boundless love of wisdom, until, growing and gaining strength on that shore, he is at last granted the vision of a single kind of knowledge, the knowledge of the beauty I will now describe; please give me your very best attention:

'"Whoever has been instructed this far in the things of love, and has learned to see beautiful things in their proper order and succession, will, as he comes toward the end, suddenly perceive something wondrously beautiful in its nature — and this, Socrates, is the goal of all our earlier efforts. In the first place, it is everlasting: it does not grow and decay, or wax and wane. Secondly, it is not beautiful from one point of view and ugly from another; not beautiful at one time, or in one relation, or in one place, and ugly at another time, or in another relation, or in another place, as if it were beautiful to some and ugly to others. Nor does it take the likeness of a face or hands or any other part of the body; nor does it take the form of any speech or knowledge; nor does it exist in any other being, such as an animal, or the heavens, or the earth, or any other place. It is absolute beauty — beauty itself, existing by itself and in itself, always one in form, and everlasting. Without growing less or greater, or changing in any way, it is shared by all the other beautiful things, which come into being and pass away. When someone rises from these through loving a young man in the right way and begins to perceive that beauty, he is not far from the end.

'"And the true order of going, or of being led by another, to the things of love is this: to begin from the beauties of earth and climb upward for the sake of that other beauty, using these only as steps — from one beautiful body to two, and from two to all beautiful bodies; from beautiful bodies to beautiful institutions, and from beautiful institutions to beautiful branches of knowledge; until from these he arrives at the knowledge of absolute beauty, and at last knows what the essence of beauty is. This, my dear Socrates," said the woman from Mantineia, "is the life above all others that a man should live, in the contemplation of absolute beauty. If you once saw that beauty, you would see that it is not to be measured against gold, and fine clothes, and beautiful boys and young men, whose presence now entrances you. You and many others would be content to live just seeing them and talking with them, without food or drink, if that were possible — you want only to look at them and to be with them. But what if a man had eyes to see the true beauty — the divine beauty, I mean, pure and clear and unmixed, not clogged with the pollutions of mortality and all the colors and empty trifles of human life? What if he could look there, and keep company with that true beauty, simple and divine?

'"Remember that only there, in that company, as he beholds beauty with the eye of the mind, will he be able to give birth not to images of beauty but to realities, because what he has hold of is not an image but a reality. And by giving birth to true virtue and nurturing it, he can become dear to the gods and be immortal, if any mortal man can. Would that be a life to despise?"

'Such, Phaedrus — and I speak not only to you, but to all of you — were the words of Diotima; and I am persuaded that they are true. And being persuaded, I try to persuade others too that, in reaching this goal, human nature will not easily find a better helper than Love. And so I say that every man ought to honor him, as I myself honor him. I devote myself to his ways, and I urge others to do the same; and now and always I praise the power and spirit of Love as well as I am able.
'What I have said, Phaedrus, you may call a speech in praise of Love, or anything else you please.'

chapters.title: Alcibiades
paragraphs: When Socrates had finished speaking, the company applauded. Aristophanes was starting to say something in answer to the allusion Socrates had made to his own speech, the one about lovers seeking their other half, when suddenly there was a loud knocking at the door of the house, as if a party of revelers had arrived, and the sound of a flute-girl could be heard. Agathon told the attendants to go and see who the intruders were. 'If they are friends of ours,' he said, 'invite them in; but if not, say that the drinking is over.' A little while later they heard the voice of Alcibiades, the famous Athenian politician and general, ringing through the courtyard. He was very drunk, and kept roaring and shouting, 'Where is Agathon? Take me to Agathon!' At last, propped up by the flute-girl and some of his attendants, he found his way to them. 'Greetings, friends,' he said, appearing at the door crowned with a massive garland of ivy and violets, with ribbons streaming from his head. 'Will you have a very drunk man as a companion in your revels? Or shall I just crown Agathon, which is what I came to do, and go away? I couldn't come yesterday, and that is why I am here today, with these ribbons on my head: I mean to take them off my own head and crown the head of the most beautiful and wisest of men — if I may be allowed to call him that. Will you laugh at me because I'm drunk? Laugh if you like; I know very well that I am speaking the truth. But first tell me: if I come in, will you accept the terms I mentioned, and take me in as drunk as I am?
'Will you drink with me or not?'

The company loudly begged him to take his place among them, and Agathon specially invited him. So he was led in by the people who were with him; and as he was being led in, intending to crown Agathon, he took the ribbons from his own head and held them in front of his eyes. This kept him from seeing Socrates, who made room for him, and Alcibiades took the empty place between Agathon and Socrates; and as he took the place, he embraced Agathon and crowned him. 'Take off his sandals,' said Agathon, 'and let him make a third on the same couch.'

'By all means; but who is the third partner in our revels?' said Alcibiades, turning round; and he jumped up as he caught sight of Socrates. 'By Heracles,' he said, 'what is this? Here is Socrates, always lying in wait for me, and always, as his way is, turning up in all sorts of unexpected places! And now, what have you got to say for yourself? And why are you lying here, where, I notice, you have schemed to get a place not next to a joker or lover of jokes, like Aristophanes, but next to the most beautiful person here?'

Socrates turned to Agathon and said: 'I must ask you to protect me, Agathon, because this man's passion has become quite a serious matter for me. Ever since I became his admirer, I have never been allowed to talk to anyone else who is beautiful, or so much as look at them. If I do, he goes wild with envy and jealousy; he not only insults me but can barely keep from hitting me, and at this very moment he may do me some harm. Please see to this: either reconcile me with him, or, if he turns violent, protect me, because I am in physical fear of his mad and passionate attacks.'

'There can never be any reconciliation between you and me,' said Alcibiades, 'but for now I'll put off punishing you. And I must ask you, Agathon, to give me back some of the ribbons, so that I can crown the marvelous head of this universal despot. I don't want him complaining that I crowned you and neglected him, when in conversation he is the conqueror of all mankind — and not just once, as you were in the theater the day before yesterday, but always.' Then, taking some of the ribbons, he crowned Socrates, and lay down again.

Then he said: 'You seem, my friends, to be sober, and that can't be allowed. You must drink — that was the agreement on which I was let in — and I appoint myself master of the drinking until you are well and truly drunk. Let's have a large goblet, Agathon — or rather,' he said to the attendant, 'bring me that wine-cooling bowl.' The bowl that had caught his eye held more than two quarts. He filled it and drained it, and told the attendant to fill it again for Socrates. 'Notice, my friends,' said Alcibiades, 'that this clever trick of mine will have no effect on Socrates, for he can drink any amount of wine and not be one bit nearer to being drunk.' Socrates drank the cup that the attendant filled for him.
Eryximachus said: 'What is this, Alcibiades? Are we to have neither conversation nor singing over our cups, but simply to drink as if we were thirsty?'
Alcibiades replied: 'Greetings, worthy son of a most wise and worthy father!'
'The same to you,' said Eryximachus; 'but what shall we do?'
'That I leave to you,' said Alcibiades.
'"The wise physician skilled our wounds to heal"
'shall prescribe, and we will obey. What do you want?'

'Well,' said Eryximachus, 'before you arrived we had passed a resolution that each of us in turn, going round from left to right, should make a speech in praise of love, the best he could. All of us have spoken; you have not spoken, but you have drunk your fill, so you ought to speak. Then you can set Socrates any task you like, and he can set one for his neighbor on the right, and so on.'

'That is good, Eryximachus,' said Alcibiades, 'and yet it is hardly fair to compare a drunk man's speech with the speeches of sober men. And I would like to know, my dear friend, whether you really believe what Socrates was saying just now. I can assure you that the exact opposite is true, and that if I praise anyone but him in his presence, whether god or man, he will hardly be able to keep from hitting me.'
'Watch what you say!' said Socrates.
'Be quiet,' said Alcibiades. 'By Poseidon, there is no one else I will praise when you are here.'
'Well then,' said Eryximachus, 'praise Socrates, if you like.'
'What do you think, Eryximachus?' said Alcibiades. 'Shall I attack him and inflict the punishment before you all?'
'What are you up to?' said Socrates. 'Are you going to raise a laugh at my expense? Is that the meaning of your praise?'
'I am going to speak the truth, if you will permit me.'
'I not only permit it; I urge you to speak the truth.'

'Then I will begin at once,' said Alcibiades, 'and if I say anything that is not true, you may interrupt me if you like and say, "That is a lie," though my intention is to speak the truth. But don't be surprised if I jump around, saying things as they come into my head, because listing all your oddities smoothly and in order is not an easy task for a man in my condition.

'And now, my friends, I shall praise Socrates by means of an image, which he will take for a caricature; but I am not using it to make fun of him, only for the sake of the truth. I say that he is exactly like the busts of Silenus, the pot-bellied old satyr, that you see set up in the sculptors' shops, holding pipes and flutes in their mouths. They are hollow and made to open down the middle, and inside them are images of gods. I say also that he is like Marsyas the satyr, the legendary flute-player. You yourself won't deny, Socrates, that your face looks like a satyr's. Yes, and you resemble them in other ways too. For example, you are insolent, as I can prove with witnesses, if you won't confess it. And aren't you a flute-player? You certainly are, and a far more wonderful performer than Marsyas. He, it is true, used instruments to charm people's souls with the power of his breath, and anyone who plays his music still does so today. For the melodies of the musician Olympus, Marsyas's pupil, come from Marsyas, who taught them to him; and these melodies, whether a great master plays them or a second-rate flute-girl, have a power that no others have. They alone take possession of the soul, and they reveal which listeners are in need of the gods and their secret rites, because the melodies themselves are divine. But you produce the same effect with words alone, without needing a flute. That is the difference between you and him.

'When we hear any other speaker, even a very good one, he has absolutely no effect on us, or not much; but mere fragments of you and your words, even at second hand, and however badly repeated, amaze and possess the souls of every man, woman, and child who hears them. And if I weren't afraid you would think me hopelessly drunk, I would swear on oath, and not just tell you, what an effect your words have always had on me, and still have. For when I hear them, my heart leaps inside me even more than the hearts of the Corybantian revelers — those worshipers who dance in a religious frenzy — and my eyes rain tears. And I see that many others are affected in the same way. I have heard the statesman Pericles and other great orators, and I thought they spoke well, but I never felt anything like this; my soul was not stirred by them, nor was I angry at the thought of my own slavish state. But this Marsyas here has often driven me to the point where I felt I could hardly bear to go on living the life I lead — this, Socrates, you will admit. And I know that if I did not stop my ears against him and flee, as from the Sirens' song, the same thing would happen to me as to others: he would hold me transfixed, and I would grow old sitting at his feet. For he makes me confess that I ought not to live as I do, neglecting the needs of my own soul and busying myself with the affairs of the Athenians. So I hold my ears and tear myself away from him.

'And he is the only person who has ever made me feel ashamed — which you might think was not in my nature — and no one else does. For I know that I cannot argue with him or say that I should not do what he tells me; but when I leave him, my love of popularity gets the better of me. So I run away from him and escape, and when I see him I am ashamed of what I have confessed to him. Many times I have wished he were dead, and yet I know that if he died I would be much more sorry than glad; so I am at my wit's end.

'And this is what I and many others have suffered from the flute-playing of this satyr. But hear me once more, while I show you how exact the image is, and how marvelous his power. For let me tell you, none of you knows him; but I will reveal him to you. Having begun, I must go on. Do you see how he is drawn to beautiful young men? He is always around them, always being smitten by them; and then again, he knows nothing and is ignorant of everything. That is the appearance he puts on. Isn't he like a Silenus in this? Of course he is. His outer mask is the carved head of the Silenus; but, my fellow drinkers, when he is opened up, what self-control you find inside! Believe me, beauty and wealth and honor, which most people marvel at, count for nothing with him; he utterly despises them. He does not care at all about the people who have them; human beings are nothing to him; he spends his whole life mocking and scorning them. But when I opened him up and looked inside at his serious purpose, I saw in him divine and golden images of such fascinating beauty that I was ready to do in a moment whatever Socrates commanded. Others may not have noticed them, but I saw them. Now, I imagined that he was seriously in love with my beauty, and I thought this would give me a grand opportunity to hear him tell me everything he knew; for I had a wonderfully high opinion of my youthful charms.

'To carry out this plan, the next time I went to see him I sent away the attendant who usually came with me. I will confess the whole truth, and I beg you to listen; and if I say anything false, you, Socrates, must expose it. Well, he and I were alone together, and I thought that now, with nobody else there, I would hear him speak to me the way a lover speaks to his beloved when they are alone, and I was delighted. Nothing of the sort. He talked with me as usual, spent the day with me, and then went away. Next I challenged him to a match at the wrestling school, and he wrestled and grappled with me several times with no one else there; I imagined I might get somewhere that way. Not a bit of it; I got nowhere with him. Finally, since I had failed so far, I thought I must take stronger measures and go after him boldly: since I had started, I would not give up on him, but would find out how matters stood between him and me. So I invited him to dinner, just as if our roles were reversed and he were the beautiful youth and I the older lover with designs on him. He was not easily persuaded to come, but after a while he did accept the invitation. The first time he came, he wanted to leave as soon as dinner was over, and I didn't have the nerve to keep him. The second time, still following my plan, I went on talking with him after dinner far into the night, and when he wanted to go, I made the excuse that it was late and that he had much better stay.

'So he lay down on the couch next to me, the same couch he had reclined on at dinner, and no one but the two of us was sleeping in the room. All this could be told to anyone without shame. But what comes next I could hardly tell you if I were sober. Still, as the proverb says, "In vino veritas": in wine there is truth. Another saying has it that wine and children both tell the truth; so wine tells the truth with children or without them, and therefore I must speak. Nor, again, would it be right for me to hide the lofty conduct of Socrates when I have set out to praise him. What's more, I have felt the serpent's bite; and a man who has been bitten, as they say, is willing to talk about it only to his fellow sufferers, because they alone are likely to understand him, and will not judge too harshly the things his agony drove him to say or do. For I have been bitten by something worse than a viper. In my soul, or in my heart, or in some other part of me, I have known the worst pang of all, which bites a gifted young mind more painfully than any serpent's tooth: the pang of philosophy, which will make a man say or do anything. And all of you I see around me — Phaedrus and Agathon and Eryximachus and Pausanias and Aristodemus and Aristophanes, and I need not mention Socrates himself — all of you have experienced the same madness and passion in your longing for wisdom. So listen, and forgive what I did then and what I am saying now. But, as at the sacred mysteries, let the attendants and anyone else who is uninitiated or ill-mannered close up the doors of their ears.

'When the lamp was put out and the servants had gone away, I thought I must speak plainly to him and put an end to the ambiguity. So I gave him a shake and said, "Socrates, are you asleep?" "No," he said. "Do you know what I have in mind?" "What do you have in mind?" he said. "I think," I replied, "that of all the lovers who have ever courted me, you are the only one who is worthy of me, and you seem too modest to speak up. Now, I feel that I would be a fool to refuse you this or any other favor, and so I have come to lay at your feet everything I have and everything my friends have, in the hope that you will help me along the way of virtue. That is what I desire above all things, and I believe you can help me in it better than anyone else. And I would certainly be more ashamed of what wise men would say if I refused a favor to a man like you than of what the world, which is mostly fools, would say about me if I granted it." He answered in the ironic manner that is so characteristic of him: "Alcibiades, my friend, you are aiming high indeed, if what you say is true, and if there really is some power in me that can make you better. You must see in me some rare beauty, of a kind infinitely higher than any I see in you. So if you mean to share with me and exchange beauty for beauty, you will get much the better of the bargain: you will gain true beauty in return for the appearance of beauty — like Diomede in Homer, who got gold armor in exchange for bronze.

'"But look again, my dear friend, and see whether you are not mistaken about me. The mind's eye begins to see sharply when the body's eyes begin to fail, and you have a long way to go before you are old." When I heard this, I said, "I have told you what I intend, and I am entirely serious. Now you decide what you think is best for you and me." "That is good," he said. "Some other time, then, we will think it over and do what seems best, about this and about other matters." At that, I imagined he was smitten, and that the words I had let fly like arrows had wounded him. So, without waiting to hear more, I got up, threw my coat around him, and crept under his threadbare cloak, since it was winter; and there I lay the whole night with this wonderful monster, this extraordinary being, in my arms. You won't deny this either, Socrates. And yet, in spite of everything, he was so unmoved by my advances, so contemptuous and mocking and disdainful of my beauty — which I really thought had some attractions! Hear me, judges, for you shall be the judges of Socrates' haughty virtue: nothing more happened. When I woke up in the morning — let all the gods and goddesses be my witnesses — I got up as if I had been sleeping beside a father or an elder brother.

'What do you suppose I felt after this rejection, at the thought of my own humiliation? And yet I couldn't help marveling at his natural self-control and restraint and manliness. I never imagined I could meet a man like him, with such wisdom and endurance. So I could not be angry with him or give up his company, any more than I could hope to win him. For I knew very well that if steel could not wound the great warrior Ajax, still less could money wound Socrates; and the one way I had of capturing him, my good looks, had failed. So I was at my wit's end; no one was ever more hopelessly enslaved by another. All this happened before he and I went on the campaign at Potidaea, the northern city that Athens was besieging. There we ate together in the same mess, and I had the chance to observe his extraordinary power of enduring fatigue. His endurance was simply marvelous when we were cut off from our supplies and forced to go without food. On such occasions, which often happen in war, he outdid not only me but everyone; there was no one to compare with him. Yet at a festival he was the only one who could really enjoy himself. He didn't want to drink, but if he was made to, he could beat us all at it; and, amazingly, no human being had ever seen Socrates drunk. And if I'm not mistaken, his powers will be tested before long. His toughness in enduring the cold was also surprising.

'There was a severe frost — the winter there is truly tremendous — and everyone else either stayed indoors or, if they went out, wore an amazing amount of clothing, with good shoes and their feet wrapped in felt and fleeces. In the middle of all this, Socrates, barefoot on the ice and in his ordinary clothes, marched better than the other soldiers who had shoes, and they glared at him, thinking he was looking down on them.
'I have told you one tale, and now I must tell you another, which is worth hearing,
'"Of the doings and sufferings of the enduring man"

'while he was on the expedition. One morning he was thinking about something he could not resolve. He would not give it up, but went on thinking from early dawn until noon; there he stood, fixed in thought. At noon people began to notice him, and the rumor ran through the wondering crowd that Socrates had been standing there thinking about something ever since daybreak. At last, in the evening after supper, some Ionians, out of curiosity — I should explain that this was not in winter but in summer — brought out their mats and slept in the open air so that they could watch him and see whether he would stand there all night. He stood there until the following morning; and when the light returned, he offered up a prayer to the sun and went his way. I will also tell you, if you like — and indeed I am bound to tell you — about his courage in battle; for who but he saved my life? This was the battle in which I received the prize for valor: I was wounded, and he would not leave me, but rescued both me and my weapons. And it was he who ought to have received the prize for valor, which the generals wanted to give me, partly because of my rank; and I told them so — this, again, Socrates will not dispute or deny — but he was more eager than the generals that I, and not he, should have the prize.

'There was another occasion when his behavior was very remarkable: during the army's flight after our defeat at the battle of Delium, where he served in the heavy infantry. I had a better opportunity of seeing him there than at Potidaea, because I was on horseback myself, and therefore comparatively out of danger. He and the general Laches were retreating, since the troops were in flight, and I met them, told them not to lose heart, and promised to stay with them. And there you could see him, Aristophanes, just as you portray him in your comedy The Clouds, and just as he is in the streets of Athens: stalking like a pelican and rolling his eyes, calmly surveying enemies as well as friends, and making it obvious to anyone, even from a distance, that whoever attacked him would be likely to meet with stout resistance. That is how he and his companion got away. For in war this is the sort of man who is never touched; the only ones who get pursued are those running away headlong. I particularly noticed how much more presence of mind he had than Laches. I could tell of many marvels in praise of Socrates. Most of his ways might perhaps be matched in another man, but his absolute unlikeness to any human being who is alive now or who has ever lived is perfectly astonishing.

'You might imagine that the Spartan general Brasidas and others were like Achilles; or you might imagine that Nestor and Antenor, Homer's wise old counselors, were like the statesman Pericles; and the same may be said of other famous men. But you will never be able to find any likeness to this strange being, however remote, either among men who live now or among those who have ever lived — other than the one I have already suggested, Silenus and the satyrs. They are an image not only of him, but of his words. For, although I forgot to mention this before, his words are like those Silenus busts that open up. When you first hear them, they sound ridiculous. He wraps himself in language like the skin of an insolent satyr: he talks about pack-donkeys and blacksmiths and cobblers and leather-workers, and he is always saying the same things in the same words, so that any ignorant or inexperienced person might feel inclined to laugh at him. But anyone who opens the bust and sees what is inside will find that his are the only words with any meaning in them, and also the most divine, full of beautiful images of virtue, and of the widest scope — or rather, reaching to the whole duty of a good and honorable man.

'That, my friends, is my praise of Socrates. I have also added my blame of him, for the way he has mistreated me; and he has mistreated not only me but Charmides the son of Glaucon, and Euthydemus the son of Diocles, and many others in the same way. He starts out as their lover, the older man courting them, and ends up making them court him instead. So I tell you, Agathon: "Don't be deceived by him. Learn from me and take warning, and don't be like the fool in the proverb, who learns only by getting hurt."'

When Alcibiades had finished, there was laughter at his frankness, because he seemed to be still in love with Socrates. 'You are sober, Alcibiades,' said Socrates, 'or you would never have gone to such roundabout lengths to hide the purpose of all this praise of your satyr. For this whole long story is just an ingenious detour, and its real point is slipped in at the end as if in passing: you want to stir up a quarrel between me and Agathon. Your idea is that I ought to love you and nobody else, and that you, and you only, ought to love Agathon. But the plot of this satyr play of yours — this Silenus drama, like the bawdy comic pieces staged after the tragedies — has been found out, and you must not let him, Agathon, turn us against each other.'

'I believe you are right,' said Agathon, 'and I suspect that he placed himself between you and me only to divide us. But he won't gain anything by that move, for I will come and lie on the couch next to you.'
'Yes, yes,' replied Socrates, 'by all means come here and lie below me, in the place on my right.'
'Oh no,' said Alcibiades, 'how this man fools me! He is determined to get the better of me at every turn. I beg you, let Agathon lie between us.'

'Certainly not,' said Socrates. 'Each of us is to praise his neighbor on the right. You have praised me, so now it is my turn to praise mine. If Agathon lay between us, he would be out of order, praising me again when he ought rather to be praised by me. So I must ask you to agree to this and not be jealous, for I have a great desire to praise the young man.'
'Hooray!' cried Agathon. 'I'll get up at once, so that Socrates can praise me.'

'The usual thing,' said Alcibiades. 'Wherever Socrates is, no one else has any chance with the beautiful young men. And now look how readily he has invented a specious reason for drawing Agathon to himself.'

Agathon was getting up to take a place on the couch beside Socrates when suddenly a crowd of revelers burst in, throwing the whole party into confusion. Someone leaving had left the front door open, and they poured in without ceremony. All order vanished, and everyone was forced to drink large quantities of wine. Aristodemus said that Eryximachus, Phaedrus, and some others left at that point, while he himself fell asleep and slept for a long time — the nights were long at that season. He woke near dawn, as the cocks were crowing, and saw that most of the company were either asleep or had gone. Only Agathon, Aristophanes, and Socrates were still awake, drinking from a large bowl that they passed around. Socrates was arguing with them. Aristodemus couldn't remember most of what was said — he'd missed the beginning and was still half asleep — but the gist was that Socrates was forcing them to admit that the gift for writing comedy was the same as the gift for writing tragedy, and that a true master of tragedy must also be a master of comedy. They were being compelled to agree, though they weren't entirely following the argument and kept nodding off. Aristophanes fell asleep first, and then, as daylight was breaking, Agathon. Socrates, having put them both to sleep, got up and left. Aristodemus followed him, as was his habit. Socrates went to the Lyceum, bathed, and spent the rest of the day as usual. In the evening, he went home to bed.
